resources.string: Remove trackers from links before you share them.
Paste a link, or any text with links
Short link expanded to its real address.
This is a short link, so its trackers are hidden. Turn on “Expand short links” to clean where it leads.
Nothing to clean on the clipboard.
No app found to open this link.
In X, Spotify, Instagram, Temu or any app, tap Share and choose “Clean link”. The clean link is copied, and the share menu opens again so you can send it on.
Select a link and pick “Clean link” from the menu. In a text box, the link is replaced in place.
Copy a link, then tap the tile: the clean link replaces it on your clipboard.
Follow t.co, temu.to, vm.tiktok.com and similar links to clean the real address. This contacts the short link\'s server; no cookies are sent.
When you share to BorraLoco, just copy the clean link without reopening the share menu.
BorraLoco appears as a browser. Make it your default browser and each tapped link is cleaned, then opened in your real browser or app.
Plus utm_*, fbclid, gclid and other common trackers on every website.
Each time you open BorraLoco, look for a new version on GitHub and offer to install it.
Couldn’t check for updates. Check your connection.
The update couldn’t be downloaded. Check your connection and try again.
Allow BorraLoco to install apps, then come back to finish the update.
Not a web link, so nothing was opened.
Stopped: the link redirects in a circle.
Stopped: the next step points to your own network, so it was not requested.
To follow short links, this contacted the link\'s servers. Nothing else was sent anywhere.
To follow short links, this contacted the link\'s servers. The site name (only) was also sent to Cloudflare\'s malware-blocking DNS.
No warning signs does not mean a link is safe. These are quick checks, not a guarantee. When in doubt, don\'t enter passwords or payment details.
Also check site names with Cloudflare
When inspecting a link, ask Cloudflare\'s malware-blocking DNS about the site name. Only the site name is sent, never the full link. Off by default.
This doesn\'t look like a web link.
This is not a normal web link: it starts with "%1$s:", which can run code or hide content.
This link tells Android to open an app with extra instructions.
This link opens an app ("%1$s:"), not a website.
The connection is not encrypted (http, not https).
Text before an "@" in the address hides the real site. The link goes somewhere else than it appears to.
The link uses a number address instead of a site name.
The address is a number written in a disguised way.
The address points to a device on your own network or phone, not the internet.
The site name contains hidden encoded characters.
The site name mixes letters from different alphabets, a trick to imitate another site.
The site name uses non-English letters. That can be normal, but check it is the site you expect.
The name "%1$s" appears in the address, but this is not %1$s\'s own site.
Looks like a fake %1$s page: the address uses the name with words like login or verify, but it is not %1$s\'s site.
The site name looks like a misspelling of %1$s.
The ending "%1$s" is often used by throwaway sites.
The ending ".%1$s" looks like a file type, a known trick.
The address has an unusually long chain of parts before the real site name.
The site name is unusually long.
The site name has many hyphens, common in fake sites.
The link uses an unusual port (%1$s).
The link downloads a program or installer (%1$s).
This is a short link; it hides its destination until opened.
This link passes through a tracking or redirect page first.
A malware-blocking DNS service (Cloudflare) blocks this site.
